blocks.content: An order is placed. The email service sends a receipt, the analytics service records the sale, the warehouse service starts packing, and the fraud service runs a check. All four react to the same single event, and the order service does not call any of them directly. It just announces, an order was created, and moves on.

That announcement style is publish subscribe, usually shortened to pub sub. One part of the system publishes an event, and every part that cares about that event receives a copy, without the publisher knowing or caring who is listening.

It is the natural pattern whenever one thing happens and many parts of the system need to react to it. Where a message queue distributes work so each task is done once, pub sub broadcasts news so everyone interested hears it.
It is the same idea as subscribing to a newsletter or a YouTube channel. The creator publishes once, and every subscriber gets their own copy, without the creator knowing who they all are.
This pattern shows up constantly, which is why it, and its contrast with message queues, is a staple of system design interviews.
In its simplest form the publisher fires and forgets, which is exactly what makes emitting an event so cheap.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278773281-343297099.png
blocks.alt: One published event fans out to every interested subscriber, each getting its own copy

blocks.content: 1. What Publish-Subscribe Is

Publish subscribe is a messaging pattern where senders, called publishers, send messages to a named channel called a topic, and receivers, called subscribers, register interest in that topic and receive every message sent to it.

The defining feature is one to many delivery. A single published message is delivered to every subscriber of the topic, each getting its own independent copy. Ten subscribers means ten deliveries of the same event.

The publisher and subscribers are fully decoupled. The publisher does not know how many subscribers exist, who they are, or what they do. It simply publishes to a topic. Subscribers come and go without the publisher ever changing.

["Publishers send events to a topic, not to a specific receiver","Subscribers register interest in a topic and receive every event on it","One to many: each event goes to all subscribers, each with its own copy","Fully decoupled: publishers and subscribers never reference each other directly"]
items: Publishers send events to a topic, not to a specific receiver
Subscribers register interest in a topic and receive every event on it
One to many: each event goes to all subscribers, each with its own copy
Fully decoupled: publishers and subscribers never reference each other directly

blocks.title: The one line version
blocks.content: In pub sub, a publisher announces an event to a topic, and every subscriber of that topic gets its own copy, with neither side knowing about the other.

People call the messages events, because they describe something that already happened, like order.created or user.deleted, in the past tense. That framing matters, a subscriber reacts to a fact, it is not being told what to do.
An event is small and self contained: an id, a type, a timestamp, and a little data about what happened, usually as JSON. Big data lives elsewhere and the event references it.
Because the publisher only names a topic, you can wire up an entirely new part of the system just by subscribing, which is the quiet magic of the pattern.
Contrast that with a phone call, which is one to one and needs both parties present. Pub sub is more like a public announcement that anyone tuned in can hear.
2. Why Pub/Sub Exists

Picture the order flow built with direct calls. The order service would have to call the email service, the analytics service, the warehouse service, and the fraud service, one by one. It would need to know all of them, wait for all of them, and be changed every time a new one is added.
That is tight coupling, and it does not scale as a system grows. Every new reaction to an order means editing the order service, and one slow or broken dependency drags down the whole flow.

Pub sub inverts this. The order service publishes a single order created event and is done. Each interested service subscribes on its own. Adding a fifth reaction, say a loyalty points service, means writing a new subscriber, with zero changes to the order service.

["Decoupling: publishers and subscribers evolve independently","Extensibility: add a new subscriber without touching the publisher","One to many: many services react to a single event effortlessly","Resilience: a slow or failed subscriber does not block the publisher or the others"]
items: Decoupling: publishers and subscribers evolve independently
Extensibility: add a new subscriber without touching the publisher
One to many: many services react to a single event effortlessly
Resilience: a slow or failed subscriber does not block the publisher or the others

blocks.content: This is the foundation of event driven architecture, where services communicate by emitting and reacting to events rather than calling each other. It lets large systems grow by adding subscribers, not by rewiring existing services.

blocks.title: The core shift
blocks.content: Pub sub turns commands into announcements. Instead of telling specific services what to do, the publisher announces what happened, and any number of services decide for themselves how to react.

Consider how the two designs age. With direct calls, adding a loyalty service means editing and redeploying the order service. With pub sub, you deploy a new subscriber and the order service never even knows it exists.
This is why event driven systems are prized for evolvability. Teams add capabilities by listening to events that already flow, rather than by changing the services that emit them.
It does come at the price of some indirection, which we weigh later, but for one to many reactions the flexibility usually wins clearly.
3. Topics, Publishers, and Subscribers
Three concepts make up every pub sub system, and the topic is the piece that ties them together.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028629-749859002.png
blocks.alt: An event bus lets many publishers and many subscribers communicate without knowing each other

blocks.content: ["Topic: a named channel that events are published to, such as order.created or user.signup","Publisher: any service that sends events to a topic","Subscriber: any service that has registered to receive events from a topic","Broker or event bus: the system that routes each published event to all of a topic subscribers"]
items: Topic: a named channel that events are published to, such as order.created or user.signup
Publisher: any service that sends events to a topic
Subscriber: any service that has registered to receive events from a topic
Broker or event bus: the system that routes each published event to all of a topic subscribers

blocks.content: The topic is the crucial decoupling point. Publishers only know the topic name, and subscribers only know the topic name. Neither knows about the other, they meet only through the topic. This is what lets you add and remove either side freely.

At larger scale, many topics together form what is often called an event bus, a shared backbone that any service can publish to and subscribe from. It becomes the central nervous system of an event driven platform.

blocks.title: Naming topics well matters
blocks.content: Topics are usually named after the event, like order.created or payment.failed, in a consistent scheme. Good topic names make it obvious what an event means and let subscribers pick exactly what they need.

Topic granularity is a real design decision. Too coarse, like a single events topic, and every subscriber receives everything and must filter. Too fine, like a topic per tiny event, and you drown in topics. Most teams group by domain, such as order events and payment events.
Topics are often hierarchical or namespaced, like commerce.order.created, so subscribers can pick a broad or narrow slice with patterns.

A useful mental model is that a topic is a contract. Whoever publishes to it and whoever subscribes to it agree on what the events look like, and that shared understanding is what keeps a decoupled system coherent.
Getting topic design right early pays off, because renaming or resplitting topics later means coordinating every publisher and subscriber that touches them.
4. Pub/Sub vs Message Queues
This is the comparison that matters most, and getting it right is a common interview checkpoint. Both use messages and a broker, but they deliver very differently.

{"headers":["Aspect","Message Queue","Publish-Subscribe"],"rows":[["Delivery","One consumer per message","Every subscriber gets a copy"],["Purpose","Distribute work","Broadcast events"],["Add a consumer","Shares the existing load","Gets its own full copy of everything"],["Coupling","Producer sends to a queue","Publisher sends to a topic, unaware of subscribers"],["Typical use","Image resize jobs","Order created fan out"]]}

The heart of the difference is who receives a message. In a queue, a message is a task, and it should be done once, so exactly one consumer gets it. In pub sub, a message is an announcement, and everyone interested should hear it, so every subscriber gets a copy.
A quick test tells them apart. If adding a second receiver should split the work, you want a queue. If adding a second receiver should give it a full independent copy of the events, you want pub sub.

blocks.title: They combine well
blocks.content: A powerful pattern is pub sub fanning an event out to several queues, one per service. Each service gets its own copy of the event, then uses a queue and workers to process it. Broadcast on top, work distribution underneath.

On AWS this combo has a name people recognise: SNS to SQS fan out. SNS is the topic that broadcasts, and each SQS queue gives one service a private, durable copy it can process with its own workers and retries.

The reason to add the queues is durability and back pressure. Pure pub sub may drop an event for an offline subscriber, but a queue in front of each service holds the event safely until that service is ready.
So the honest one liner is that a queue divides work while pub sub duplicates news, and many systems need both at different points.
5. How a Message Is Delivered
Following one event from publish to delivery makes the model concrete.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278776686-853157163.png
blocks.alt: A published event is copied and delivered to every subscriber of the topic

blocks.content: ["A subscriber registers its interest in a topic with the broker","A publisher sends an event to that topic","The broker looks up every current subscriber of the topic","The broker delivers a copy of the event to each of them","Each subscriber processes its own copy independently"]
items: A subscriber registers its interest in a topic with the broker
A publisher sends an event to that topic
The broker looks up every current subscriber of the topic
The broker delivers a copy of the event to each of them
Each subscriber processes its own copy independently

blocks.content: The important word is copy. The broker does not hand the single event to one lucky subscriber, it delivers a separate copy to each. What one subscriber does with its copy, including failing, has no effect on the others.

This independence is a big part of pub sub value. The analytics service can be slow, the email service can be down, and the warehouse service still gets its copy and carries on. Each subscriber succeeds or fails on its own.

This is also why a subscriber being down is not a disaster in a durable system. Its copies wait, in its queue or in the retained log, and it catches up when it returns. In a fire and forget system, though, those events would simply be missed.

The flip side is that debugging spans many services. When one order event triggers five reactions, a failure could be in any of them, so tracing that follows an event across subscribers becomes important.
A single publish can quietly set off a whole cascade of independent work, which is both the power and, if unmanaged, the confusion of the pattern.
6. Delivery Models and Fan-out
Under the surface, brokers deliver to subscribers in a couple of ways, and it is worth knowing the difference.

In a push model, the broker actively sends each event to the subscribers as it arrives, for example by calling a webhook or pushing over a connection. In a pull model, subscribers ask the broker for new events when they are ready, reading from the topic at their own pace.

["Push: the broker delivers events to subscribers immediately, low latency but can overwhelm a slow subscriber","Pull: subscribers fetch events when ready, which paces the load to what each can handle","Fan-out: the broker duplicating one event to many subscribers is the defining action of pub sub"]
items: Push: the broker delivers events to subscribers immediately, low latency but can overwhelm a slow subscriber
Pull: subscribers fetch events when ready, which paces the load to what each can handle
Fan-out: the broker duplicating one event to many subscribers is the defining action of pub sub

blocks.content: The word fan-out captures the essence: one event in, many copies out. The cost of that fan-out grows with the number of subscribers, which is a real consideration when a single popular event has thousands of subscribers.

blocks.title: Fan-out has a cost
blocks.content: Delivering one event to a thousand subscribers is a thousand deliveries. At high volume this is significant work for the broker, which is why large scale pub sub systems are carefully engineered for fan-out.

Push delivery to external systems is often done over webhooks. Amazon SNS, for instance, can push each event to an HTTP endpoint, an email, or an SMS, which makes pub sub reach beyond your own services.
To protect slow subscribers under push, systems add flow control or put a queue in front, so a burst of events does not overwhelm a consumer that cannot keep up.
At truly massive fan out, systems even build trees of brokers, so one event spreads through layers rather than one broker delivering a million copies alone.
7. Consumer Groups and Scaling
Pub sub and work distribution seem to pull in opposite directions, one broadcasts and the other splits, but modern systems combine them cleanly with consumer groups.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278778354-495214601.png
blocks.alt: Each consumer group reads the whole topic independently, and splits the work among its own members

blocks.content: The idea, made famous by Kafka, is this. Each consumer group is an independent subscriber to the topic, so every group receives all the events. But within a single group, the events are split across the group members, so the work is shared.

["Between groups it behaves like pub sub: each group gets a full copy of every event","Within a group it behaves like a queue: members split the events so each is processed once by the group","Add a group to get a new independent consumer of all events","Add members to a group to process that group workload faster"]
items: Between groups it behaves like pub sub: each group gets a full copy of every event
Within a group it behaves like a queue: members split the events so each is processed once by the group
Add a group to get a new independent consumer of all events
Add members to a group to process that group workload faster

blocks.content: This gives the best of both worlds. The analytics group and the email group each get every order event, which is pub sub, while inside the analytics group ten workers share the load, which is a queue. It is why log based systems power so much of modern event processing.

Partitions are the unit of parallelism. A topic is split into partitions, and within a consumer group each partition is handled by exactly one member, so the number of partitions sets the maximum useful number of workers in a group.

When members join or leave a group, the system rebalances, reassigning partitions across the current members. This is powerful but not free, since a rebalance briefly pauses consumption, so you avoid triggering it constantly.
Choosing a good partition key matters too, because it decides both how events are spread for parallelism and which events stay ordered together.
This is why log based pub sub feels like both a broadcast system and a scalable work queue at once, and why it became the backbone of modern data platforms.
8. Message Retention and Replay
There is a deep split in pub sub systems around what happens to an event after it is delivered, and it changes what the system can do.

Traditional pub sub is fire and forget. Once an event is delivered to the current subscribers, it is gone. A subscriber that was offline, or one that is added later, never sees it. This is simple and lightweight.

Log based pub sub, like Kafka, instead keeps events in an ordered, durable log for a configured time, whether hours or forever. Subscribers read from a position in the log, and because the events are retained, a subscriber can go back and replay them.

["Traditional: events are delivered then discarded, so only current subscribers see them","Log based: events are retained, so subscribers can replay history and new subscribers can read from the start","Replay enables reprocessing after a bug fix, backfilling a new service, and rebuilding state from events","Retention costs storage, which is the tradeoff for keeping the history around"]
items: Traditional: events are delivered then discarded, so only current subscribers see them
Log based: events are retained, so subscribers can replay history and new subscribers can read from the start
Replay enables reprocessing after a bug fix, backfilling a new service, and rebuilding state from events
Retention costs storage, which is the tradeoff for keeping the history around

blocks.title: Replay is a superpower
blocks.content: The ability to replay past events is one of the biggest reasons teams choose a log based system. You can add a brand new service and feed it months of history, or fix a consumer bug and reprocess everything it got wrong.

Subscribers in a log based system track their position with an offset, a cursor into the log. Committing an offset says I have processed up to here, and on restart the subscriber resumes from that point rather than from the beginning.

Some logs also support compaction, keeping only the latest event per key. This turns the log into a compact snapshot of current state, handy for rebuilding caches or feeding a new service the current picture rather than the full history.
Retention is configured per topic, often a number of days, and it is a straight tradeoff of storage cost against how far back you can replay.
9. Filtering and Routing
Subscribers rarely want every event in the system, so pub sub systems provide ways to receive only the events that matter to them.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278779994-321907874.png
blocks.alt: A router delivers each event only to the subscribers whose interest matches it

blocks.content: ["Topic based: subscribe to specific topics, like order.created but not order.cancelled","Pattern based: subscribe with wildcards, like order.* to get every order event","Attribute or content based: the broker filters on fields in the event, delivering only matching ones","Multiple topics: split events into fine grained topics so subscribers pick exactly what they need"]
items: Topic based: subscribe to specific topics, like order.created but not order.cancelled
Pattern based: subscribe with wildcards, like order.* to get every order event
Attribute or content based: the broker filters on fields in the event, delivering only matching ones
Multiple topics: split events into fine grained topics so subscribers pick exactly what they need

blocks.content: This routing is what keeps pub sub efficient at scale. Instead of every subscriber receiving everything and filtering on its own, the broker delivers only the relevant events, which saves both network traffic and subscriber work.

RabbitMQ makes this explicit with exchanges, which route messages to queues by rules, while systems like Kafka lean on many topics and partitions. Either way, the goal is the same, get each event only to those who want it.

Content based filtering pushes this further, letting a subscriber say, for example, only order events where the amount is over one thousand. The broker evaluates the rule and delivers only matching events.
The tradeoff is that richer filtering costs the broker more work per event, so very heavy filtering is sometimes better done in the subscriber, balancing broker load against wasted delivery.
The overall aim is precision: deliver each event to those who want it and no one else, which keeps both the network and the subscribers efficient.
10. Delivery Guarantees and Ordering
Pub sub faces the same hard questions as any messaging system: can events be lost, duplicated, or reordered.

Most systems offer at least once delivery, meaning an event will reach a subscriber but might arrive more than once. As with queues, this means subscribers should be idempotent, so processing the same event twice is harmless.

Ordering is usually only guaranteed within a partition or a single topic key, not across the whole topic. Log based systems keep strict order inside each partition, so events for the same entity, routed by a key like a user id, stay in order, while different keys flow in parallel.

["At least once is the common default, so design subscribers to tolerate duplicates","Order is typically preserved per partition or per key, not globally","Route related events with the same key to keep them ordered where it matters","Exactly once processing is approximated with at least once delivery plus idempotency"]
items: At least once is the common default, so design subscribers to tolerate duplicates
Order is typically preserved per partition or per key, not globally
Route related events with the same key to keep them ordered where it matters
Exactly once processing is approximated with at least once delivery plus idempotency

blocks.title: Same lessons as queues
blocks.content: Idempotent subscribers and per key ordering are the same tools you use with message queues. The messaging guarantees do not change just because the delivery is one to many.

Kafka does offer an exactly once mode using idempotent producers and transactions, which is genuinely useful, but it adds cost and complexity and only holds within the Kafka boundary. Most teams still lean on idempotent consumers as the simpler, more general answer.
The safe stance is to treat duplicates as inevitable and design so a repeated event changes nothing the second time, then ordering and exactly once become optimisations rather than requirements.
This mirrors the queue chapter on purpose, because the underlying truth is the same: reliable messaging plus idempotency is how you get correctness in a distributed system.
11. Popular Pub/Sub Systems
The pattern is universal, but the systems that implement it differ in scale, retention, and style.

{"headers":["System","Type","Notable for"],"rows":[["Kafka","Log based streaming","High throughput, retention, replay, consumer groups"],["Google Pub/Sub","Managed","Serverless, global scale, at least once"],["Amazon SNS","Managed","Fan out to queues, email, and SMS"],["Redis Pub/Sub","In memory","Very fast and simple, but no persistence"],["RabbitMQ","Broker with exchanges","Flexible routing through exchanges"]]}

Kafka dominates high volume event streaming, where retention, replay, and consumer groups matter. Managed services like Google Pub/Sub and Amazon SNS remove the operational burden and scale automatically.

At the lighter end, Redis pub sub is fast and trivial to use but forgets events immediately, so it suits live, best effort notifications rather than durable event streams. RabbitMQ sits in the middle, a flexible broker whose exchanges give rich routing.

blocks.title: SNS plus SQS is a classic combo
blocks.content: On AWS, publishing to an SNS topic that fans out to several SQS queues is a textbook pattern: SNS broadcasts the event, and each SQS queue gives one service a durable, retryable copy to process.

For the internet of things, MQTT is the pub sub protocol of choice, built for huge numbers of low power devices publishing sensor readings to topics. NATS is another lightweight, very fast option popular in cloud native systems.
The choice usually comes down to a few questions: do you need durable retention and replay, how much throughput, is a managed service acceptable, and how rich does the routing need to be.
Redis pub sub, by contrast, is best kept for ephemeral, live signals like presence or a live counter, where losing a message now and then is harmless.
There is rarely one right answer, only the system that best fits your throughput, durability, and operational appetite.
12. When to Use Pub/Sub
Pub sub is the right tool whenever one event needs to trigger many independent reactions, or whenever you want services to stay decoupled through events.

["One event, many reactions, like an order triggering email, analytics, and fulfilment","Event driven architecture, where services emit and react to events rather than calling each other","Broadcasting state changes so many services stay in sync","Streaming and analytics pipelines that consume a shared event stream","Adding new features by subscribing to existing events, with no change to producers"]
items: One event, many reactions, like an order triggering email, analytics, and fulfilment
Event driven architecture, where services emit and react to events rather than calling each other
Broadcasting state changes so many services stay in sync
Streaming and analytics pipelines that consume a shared event stream
Adding new features by subscribing to existing events, with no change to producers

blocks.content: It is the wrong tool when work should be done once rather than by everyone, where a queue is correct, or when the caller needs an immediate answer, where a direct request is correct. Pub sub is about broadcasting facts, not fetching results.
Use pub sub when something happened and many parts of the system need to know. Use a queue when something needs to be done exactly once.

Pub sub also underpins advanced patterns like event sourcing, where the log of events is the source of truth, and CQRS, where events keep read models up to date. These are advanced, but they all rest on the same publish and subscribe foundation.

The general principle is that events become a shared, reusable stream. Once an event exists, any number of current and future services can build on it, which is a big part of why event driven design scales organizationally, not just technically.
In short, pub sub is not just a messaging trick, it is the substrate a whole style of architecture is built on.
If a requirement sounds like when X happens, several things should follow, that is almost always a pub sub shaped problem.
13. Common Mistakes and Challenges
Pub sub is powerful, but its very looseness creates its own traps.

["Assuming exactly once delivery and skipping idempotency, so duplicates cause double effects","Expecting global ordering, when only per partition or per key order is guaranteed","Ignoring fan-out cost, so a popular event with many subscribers overwhelms the broker","Losing track of who consumes what, since the decoupling that helps also hides the dependencies","Using fire and forget pub sub where you actually needed durability and replay"]
items: Assuming exactly once delivery and skipping idempotency, so duplicates cause double effects
Expecting global ordering, when only per partition or per key order is guaranteed
Ignoring fan-out cost, so a popular event with many subscribers overwhelms the broker
Losing track of who consumes what, since the decoupling that helps also hides the dependencies
Using fire and forget pub sub where you actually needed durability and replay

blocks.content: The subtle downside of pub sub is exactly its strength turned around. Because publishers do not know their subscribers, it can become hard to see what depends on an event, which makes changes risky. Good event schemas and documentation are the antidote.

blocks.title: Version your events
blocks.content: Because many unknown subscribers may depend on an event, changing its shape can break them silently. Treat event formats as a contract, version them, and evolve them carefully, just like a public API.

A schema registry is the common tool for this. Publishers register the shape of each event, subscribers validate against it, and the registry enforces compatible evolution, so a bad change is caught before it breaks anyone.

Because dependencies are hidden, observability matters more here than with direct calls. Distributed tracing that follows an event through its subscribers, and dashboards of who consumes each topic, restore the visibility that decoupling takes away.
Treating events as a first class, documented part of your system, rather than an afterthought, is what separates a clean event driven design from a tangled one.
14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: When a design has one event that many services must react to, pub sub is the answer, and the interviewer wants to hear how it differs from a queue and how you handle its pitfalls.
Contrast with a queue: I use pub sub when every interested service needs its own copy of an event, and a queue when a task should be done once.
Lead with decoupling: The publisher just announces an event to a topic, so I can add new subscribers later without touching it, which is the core of event driven design.
Combine broadcast and work: I use consumer groups so each group gets all events while sharing the load among its members, getting fan out and scaling together.
Handle the guarantees: I assume at least once delivery and make subscribers idempotent, rely on per key ordering, and version event schemas since many unknown subscribers depend on them.
Name the tradeoff: I point out that pub sub trades visibility for flexibility, so I add event versioning, a schema registry, and tracing to keep a loosely coupled system understandable.
